weeks.1: The basics: owning a slice of a company
weeks.2: Who gives startups money, step by step
weeks.3: The investor's side: how a VC fund works
weeks.4: What investors look at before they say yes
weeks.5: The deal: cap tables and term sheets
weeks.6: Endgame: exits, bad days, India, thinking like a VC

lessons.title: Why startups need a different kind of money
lessons.idea: A startup trades a slice of its future for money today, because no bank will lend to an idea.
explain: A normal business, like a kirana shop, can borrow from a bank. The bank checks that the shop already earns money and can repay the loan with interest.

A startup is different. It is a young company trying to grow very fast, usually losing money for years first. A bank won't lend to it, because there's nothing to repay the loan with yet and a high chance it fails.

So startups raise money a different way. Instead of borrowing, they sell a small piece of ownership in the company. The buyer doesn't get repaid. They win only if the company becomes very valuable, and they lose everything if it dies.
This is called equity funding. Venture capital (VC) is the industry that does this for a living.
lessons.ex_title: Meet ChaiCart (made up, and we'll follow it for 6 weeks)
ex: Riya and Arjun in Mumbai have an idea: deliver hot chai and snacks to offices in 10 minutes.
They need about ₹50 lakh to hire 4 people, build an app and run a pilot in 20 offices.
A bank asks: 'What do you earn today?' Answer: nothing. Loan refused.
So they will sell a slice of ChaiCart instead. Over the next lessons you'll see how big a slice, to whom, and at what price.
lessons.investors: Investors aren't asking 'will this repay me?' They're asking 'could this become huge?' A small chance of a giant outcome is worth more to them than a safe, small one.
lessons.q: Why does a VC accept that most of its startups will fail?
lessons.a: Because it isn't lending. It owns slices, and one company becoming enormous can pay for all the failures many times over. We'll see the maths in Week 3.

lessons.title: Equity: owning slices of the pie
lessons.idea: A company is divided into shares. Whoever holds a share owns that fraction of the company.
explain: When a company is created, it issues shares, like cutting a pizza into slices. The number is arbitrary: 100 shares or 10 lakh shares work the same way.
Your ownership percentage = your shares ÷ all shares. That percentage is what matters, not the raw count.
If the company is ever sold, or earns profits it pays out, owners get money in proportion to their percentage.
Founders usually start owning 100% between them. Every time they raise money, they create new shares for investors, so the pizza gets cut into more slices.
ex: ChaiCart is registered as a private limited company with 10,00,000 (10 lakh) shares.
Riya gets 5,00,000 and Arjun gets 5,00,000. Each owns 50%.
lessons.investors: Investors always ask 'what % will I own?' and 'how many shares exist in total, counting promises like employee stock options?' The second question catches many founders out.
lessons.q: If ChaiCart had issued 100 shares instead of 10 lakh, would anything important change?
lessons.a: No. Riya and Arjun would still own 50% each. Only the percentage matters; the share count just sets the price per share.

lessons.title: Valuation: what is a company worth before it earns anything?
lessons.idea: A startup's valuation isn't calculated from profits. It's a price the founders and an investor agree on.
explain: For a mature company, value comes from its profits: an investor might pay 20 times what it earns a year.

A young startup has no profits, so its valuation is mostly a negotiation. The inputs are: how strong the team is, how big the opportunity is, early signs that customers love it, and how many other investors want in.
Think of it like an auction for a painting by an unknown artist. There's no 'correct' price; it's what someone is willing to pay, shaped by how many buyers turn up.
In practice, investors work backwards: 'I want about 10–20% of this company for my cheque. If my cheque is ₹50 lakh, the company must be worth roughly ₹2.5–5 crore.'
ex: An angel investor, Mr Mehta, likes ChaiCart. He wants to invest ₹50 lakh and own 10%.
If ₹50 lakh buys 10%, the whole company (after his money comes in) must be worth ₹50 lakh ÷ 10% = ₹5 crore.
Nobody 'calculated' ₹5 crore from profits. It came from how much he wanted to put in and how much he wanted to own.
lessons.investors: Investors care less about today's valuation than about whether the company can be worth 10–100 times more later. A slightly high price on a winner is fine; a cheap price on a loser is worthless.
lessons.q: Mehta invests ₹1 crore for 20%. What is the company worth after his investment?
lessons.a: ₹1 crore ÷ 20% = ₹5 crore. Same value, bigger cheque, bigger slice.

lessons.title: Pre-money and post-money: the most important formula
lessons.idea: Pre-money is the value before the new cash comes in. Post-money is pre-money plus the cash.
explain: When someone invests, the company's value jumps by exactly the cash they put in, because that cash now sits in the company's bank account.
Pre-money valuation = what the company is worth just before the investment.
Post-money valuation = pre-money + new investment.
Investor's ownership = investment ÷ post-money. Always divide by post-money, because the investor owns a slice of the company including their own cash.
Mixing up pre and post is the most common beginner mistake, and it changes who owns what.
ex: Mehta and the founders agree on a pre-money of ₹4.5 crore.
Mehta invests ₹50 lakh. Post-money = ₹4.5 crore + ₹0.5 crore = ₹5 crore.
Mehta owns ₹0.5 crore ÷ ₹5 crore = 10%.
Price per share = pre-money ÷ existing shares = ₹4.5 crore ÷ 10,00,000 = ₹45 per share.
So Mehta gets ₹50,00,000 ÷ ₹45 = 1,11,111 new shares. Total shares are now 11,11,111.
lessons.investors: Investors always confirm in writing whether a number is pre or post. '₹5 crore valuation' can mean Mehta owns 10% (if post) or about 9.1% (if pre: 0.5 ÷ 5.5).
lessons.q: A startup raises ₹2 crore at a ₹8 crore pre-money. What's the post-money, and what % does the investor own?
lessons.a: Post-money = 8 + 2 = ₹10 crore. Investor owns 2 ÷ 10 = 20%.

lessons.title: Dilution: a smaller slice of a bigger pie
lessons.idea: Every new round shrinks the founders' percentage, but if the price went up, their slice is worth more.
explain: When new shares are created for an investor, everyone else's percentage goes down. This is called dilution.
Dilution isn't a loss by itself. Owning 50% of a ₹1 crore company (₹50 lakh) is worse than owning 30% of a ₹100 crore company (₹30 crore).
Quick rule: after a round where the new investor gets X%, every existing owner keeps (100% − X%) of what they had. If the investor gets 20%, everyone keeps 80% of their old percentage.
Dilution becomes a real problem only when it's too much too early, or when a round happens at a lower price than before (a 'down round', Week 6).
lessons.ex_title: What Mehta's 10% did to the founders
ex: Before: Riya 50%, Arjun 50%.
Mehta gets 10%, so the founders keep 90% of their old stake: 50% × 0.9 = 45% each.
But each founder's stake is now worth 45% × ₹5 crore = ₹2.25 crore on paper, with real cash in the bank to grow.
lessons.investors: Investors want founders to keep a meaningful stake (often over 50% combined after the Series A) so they stay motivated for the next 8–10 years.
lessons.q: A founder owns 40% and the next investor takes 25%. What does the founder own afterwards?

lessons.title: Bootstrapping, and friends and family money
lessons.idea: The very first money usually comes from the founders' own savings, or people who know them.
explain: Bootstrapping means building with your own money and the company's own revenue, with no outside investors. You keep 100%, but growth is limited by what you can afford.
Friends and family rounds are small cheques from people who trust the founder more than the idea. They often don't negotiate hard on price.
The risk: these investors may not understand that most startups fail. Good founders explain clearly that this money could be lost completely.
Many great companies, like Zerodha in India, grew largely bootstrapped. Raising VC money isn't compulsory; it's a choice to grow faster in exchange for ownership.
ex: Riya and Arjun put in ₹5 lakh each of savings to build a basic app and test in 3 offices near their home.
Those 3 offices order every day, which is the proof that convinced Mehta later.
They chose not to take money from relatives, to avoid awkward Diwali dinners if it failed.
lessons.investors: Investors like founders who've put in their own money and got early proof cheaply. It shows commitment and resourcefulness.
lessons.q: What do founders give up by bootstrapping, and what do they keep?
lessons.a: They give up speed (less money to hire and market). They keep full ownership and control.

lessons.title: Angel investors
lessons.idea: Angels are wealthy individuals who invest their own money in very early startups, often before there's a real product.
explain: An angel is usually a successful founder, executive or professional investing personal money, typically lakhs to a couple of crores per startup.
Angels bet on people. At this stage there's little data, so they ask: do I trust these founders to figure things out?
Good angels bring more than money: advice, introductions to customers and to VCs for the next round.
In India, angels often invest through angel networks or platforms, where many people pool small cheques into one deal and share the research.
ex: Mehta used to run a large office-catering business. He knows offices hate their tea vending machines.
He saw that 3 offices ordered daily for 2 months without any discount. That's real demand.
He invested ₹50 lakh for 10% (at ₹5 crore post-money) and introduced ChaiCart to 15 more offices from his old network.
lessons.investors: Angels look at the founders, the founders' insight into the problem, and any early sign that customers truly want it.
lessons.q: Why might an angel invest in a startup with no revenue?
lessons.a: Because they're betting on the founders and an early sign of demand, and the price is low enough that a big success would return many times their money.

lessons.title: The seed round
lessons.idea: Seed money turns a promising pilot into a real business that can show steady growth.
explain: After angels, the next step is usually a seed round: a few crore rupees from seed-focused VC funds, accelerators and angels.
Accelerators (like Y Combinator in the US) give a small amount of money, a few months of coaching and a 'demo day' in exchange for a few percent of the company.
The goal of seed money: find a product that customers keep using and paying for, and prove you can get more customers in a repeatable way. People call this 'product-market fit'.
Seed rounds usually sell 15–25% of the company.
ex: ChaiCart now serves 80 offices. Seedling Ventures (made up) offers ₹3 crore at a ₹12 crore pre-money.
Post-money = 12 + 3 = ₹15 crore. Seedling owns 3 ÷ 15 = 20%.
Everyone else keeps 80% of their old stake: founders 45% → 36% each; Mehta 10% → 8%.
Mehta's 8% is now worth 8% × ₹15 crore = ₹1.2 crore on paper. His ₹50 lakh has grown 2.4x in value.
lessons.investors: Seed investors look for early signs of product-market fit: are customers coming back on their own, and is usage growing week after week?
lessons.q: Why did Mehta's percentage fall but his paper value rise?
lessons.a: He was diluted from 10% to 8%, but the company's value tripled from ₹5 crore to ₹15 crore, so 8% of ₹15 crore beats 10% of ₹5 crore.

lessons.title: Series A, B, C: climbing the ladder
lessons.idea: Each lettered round is bigger, happens at a higher valuation, and expects more proof.
explain: Series A: the company has product-market fit and needs money to build a proper team and scale what works. Investors want clear numbers: revenue growth, retention, a sense of profit per customer.
Series B: the machine works; now grow fast into new cities or products.
Series C and beyond: dominate the market, expand abroad, buy smaller companies, prepare for an IPO (listing on the stock exchange).
Each round typically sells 10–25% of the company. Founders get diluted each time, but by much less if the valuation rises a lot.
ex: ChaiCart is in 600 offices across Mumbai and Pune. Growth Capital (made up) invests ₹20 crore at an ₹80 crore pre-money.
Post-money = ₹100 crore. Growth Capital owns 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.
Everyone keeps 80% of their stake again.
lessons.investors: At Series A, gut feel gives way to data. Investors check whether growth comes from customers who stay, and whether each new customer is profitable over time (Week 4).
lessons.q: Riya's stake fell from 50% to 28.8%. What's it worth now on paper?
lessons.a: 28.8% × ₹100 crore = ₹28.8 crore, compared with nothing when she owned 100% of an idea.

lessons.title: What a VC actually is
lessons.idea: A VC firm invests other people's money in startups, in exchange for fees and a share of the profits.
explain: Angels invest their own money. VC firms mostly invest money from others: pension funds, insurance companies, university endowments, family offices and rich individuals.
Those outside investors are called LPs (limited partners). They give money but don't pick the startups.
The VC partners who pick startups and manage the money are called GPs (general partners).
So a VC has two sets of customers: founders, whom they must win deals from, and LPs, whom they must return money to. Everything a VC does makes sense once you remember they answer to their LPs.
ex: Growth Capital runs a ₹500 crore fund.
₹480 crore came from LPs: an insurance company, two family offices and a university endowment.
₹10 crore came from the GPs themselves (GPs usually invest about 1–2% of the fund, so they have their own money at risk), plus ₹10 crore from a few successful founders.
When Growth Capital invested ₹20 crore in ChaiCart, that was really LP money, managed by the GPs.
lessons.investors: Remember the VC's own boss: LPs judge VCs on returns over about 10 years. That's why VCs push for big outcomes, not modest, safe ones.
lessons.q: Who are LPs and GPs in one line each?
lessons.a: LPs provide most of the money and stay passive. GPs run the fund, choose startups and get paid fees plus a share of profits.

lessons.title: How a VC fund is built
lessons.idea: A fund is a pot of money with a fixed life, usually about 10 years.
explain: A VC firm raises a fund, say ₹400 crore, from LPs. The fund has a lifespan of about 10 years, sometimes extended by 1–2 years.
Years 1–4ish: the investment period, when the fund makes new investments.
Years 4–10ish: the fund supports its best companies with more money and waits for exits (sales or IPOs) to return cash to LPs.
LPs don't hand over all the money on day one. The fund 'calls' it in pieces when it needs to invest (a capital call).
When one fund is mostly invested, the firm raises the next one. That's why firms have Fund I, Fund II and so on.
lessons.ex_title: Monsoon Ventures Fund I (made up, our fund for this week)
ex: Size: ₹400 crore, from 30 LPs.
Plan: back about 20 seed-stage startups over 4 years.
Keep roughly half the money in reserve to put more into the winners in later rounds.
Return cash to LPs as companies get acquired or go public, mostly in years 6–12.
lessons.investors: Because a fund has a deadline, VCs need companies that can exit within about 7–10 years. A great business that will never be sold or listed doesn't fit a VC fund.
lessons.q: Why don't VCs invest in a profitable family business that will never be sold?
lessons.a: Because the fund must return cash to its LPs within about 10 years, and the fund only gets cash back when its stake is sold.

lessons.title: 2 and 20: how VCs get paid
lessons.idea: VCs charge about 2% a year to run the fund, and keep about 20% of the profits.
explain: Management fee: about 2% of the fund each year, used for salaries, offices and research. Over 10 years that adds up to a big chunk, which is why fees usually drop after the investment period.

Carried interest ('carry'): the GPs keep about 20% of the profits, but only after LPs get back all the money they put in. Many funds, including many in India, also promise LPs a minimum return (a 'hurdle', often around 8% a year) before carry kicks in.
So GPs get rich only if LPs do well first. This aligns everyone, in theory.
ex: Fund size: ₹400 crore. Fees over the life: roughly ₹60–80 crore (say ₹70 crore), so about ₹330 crore actually gets invested.
Suppose the investments return ₹1,200 crore in total.
Profit = ₹1,200 crore − ₹400 crore returned to LPs first = ₹800 crore.
Carry to GPs = 20% × ₹800 crore = ₹160 crore. LPs get ₹400 + ₹640 = ₹1,040 crore.
LPs turned ₹400 crore into ₹1,040 crore: 2.6x their money, after all fees and carry.
lessons.investors: LPs compare the fund's returns after fees and carry with simply buying a stock index. A VC fund needs to beat that clearly to be worth the risk and the 10-year lock-in.
lessons.q: If Monsoon returned exactly ₹400 crore in total, how much carry would the GPs get?
lessons.a: Zero. LPs must get their ₹400 crore back first, and there's no profit left to share. The GPs would only have earned the management fees.

lessons.title: The power law: one winner pays for everything
lessons.idea: In venture, a tiny number of companies make almost all the returns.
explain: In most of life, results cluster around the average. In venture, results follow a 'power law': most investments return little or nothing, and one or two return enormous amounts.
This changes how VCs think. Missing the one big winner is far worse than backing ten failures.
So a VC's key question about every startup is: 'If everything goes right, could this be big enough to return my whole fund?'
That's why VCs can seem to ignore nice, safe businesses: a company that can at most triple won't move a fund.
lessons.ex_title: Monsoon's 20 seed investments of ₹10 crore each (₹200 crore)
ex: 12 companies fail: ₹0 back.
5 limp along and are sold for about what was invested: ₹50 crore back.
2 do well and return 5x: ₹100 crore back.
1 becomes huge and returns 50x: ₹500 crore back.
Total: ₹650 crore from ₹200 crore, or 3.25x. Remove that one winner and it's ₹150 crore, a loss.
lessons.investors: Investors size up the 'best case' first. A pitch that only shows a safe, modest outcome loses VCs, even if it's very likely to succeed.
lessons.q: Without its single best company, did Monsoon make or lose money?
lessons.a: Lose: ₹150 crore back on ₹200 crore invested. One winner turned a loss into a 3.25x result.

lessons.title: Measuring a fund: TVPI, DPI and IRR
lessons.idea: Paper gains and cash in hand are different things, and timing matters.
explain: TVPI (total value to paid-in): everything the fund is worth today, including shares not yet sold, divided by what LPs paid in. It includes paper gains.
DPI (distributions to paid-in): actual cash returned to LPs divided by what they paid in. LPs love DPI because it's real money, not estimates.
IRR (internal rate of return): the yearly growth rate of the money. Getting 3x in 5 years is much better than 3x in 12 years.
Early in a fund's life, TVPI can look great while DPI is close to zero. Over time the gap should close as companies are sold.
ex: Monsoon invested ₹10 crore in a startup.
After 5 years it sold some shares for ₹5 crore of cash and still holds shares valued at ₹25 crore.
DPI = ₹5 crore ÷ ₹10 crore = 0.5x (half the money is back as cash).
TVPI = (₹5 crore + ₹25 crore) ÷ ₹10 crore = 3x.
IRR: tripling in 5 years is about 25% a year, if the paper value turns into cash.
lessons.investors: LPs ask 'what's your DPI?' because paper values can be optimistic. A fund with high TVPI but no DPI after 8 years worries them.
lessons.q: Why might an LP prefer a fund with 2x DPI over one with 4x TVPI and 0.2x DPI?
lessons.a: Because 2x DPI is real cash already returned, while 4x TVPI is mostly valuations that may never turn into cash.

lessons.title: Building a portfolio: how many bets, and how much in reserve
lessons.idea: VCs plan how many startups to back and save money to double down on the winners.
explain: A fund decides upfront roughly how many companies to back (often 20–40), how big each first cheque is, and what ownership it targets (often 10–20% at entry).
It also keeps 'reserves', often 40–60% of the fund, to invest again in later rounds of the companies that are working. This is called follow-on investing.
Pro-rata rights let an investor buy enough new shares in later rounds to keep its percentage. Using them on winners is how funds keep meaningful ownership.
The hard skill is deciding where to put reserves: back the winners, not rescue the strugglers.
ex: Seedling owned 20% after the seed round and would be diluted to 16% in the Series A.
Its pro-rata right let it buy 20% of the new Series A shares: about ₹4 crore (20% of the ₹20 crore round), which would have kept it at 20%.
In our story, Seedling chose to save its reserves for later, so it was diluted to 16%. The next round would show whether that was wise.
lessons.investors: Founders should know which of their investors have reserves and pro-rata rights. An existing investor who doesn't follow on sends a negative signal to new investors.
lessons.q: Why do funds keep so much money in reserve instead of backing more new companies?
lessons.a: Because of the power law: putting more money into the few winners earns far more than spreading it across extra early bets.

lessons.title: The team: why VCs bet on people first
lessons.idea: Early on, the founders are the main evidence a VC has.
explain: At seed stage there's little data, and the idea will probably change. Investors back people who can learn fast and adapt.
They look for 'founder-market fit': why are these people unusually well placed to win this specific market?
They also check: Can the founders sell the idea to customers, employees and investors? Do the co-founders complement each other? How did they handle past setbacks?
Red flags: one founder holding all the power with no balance, co-founders who disagree on the vision, or founders not working on it full time.
lessons.ex_title: How Growth Capital judged Riya and Arjun
ex: Riya: ex-operations manager at a food delivery company, so she knows 10-minute logistics.
Arjun: ex-sales lead selling software to office managers, so he knows how offices buy.
Their past metrics: hit monthly targets 14 months in a row, and survived a supplier collapse in month 6 without losing customers.
Verdict: strong founder-market fit.
lessons.investors: VCs ask: why you, why now, and how fast do you learn? They'll call former colleagues, customers and even ex-employees to check.
lessons.q: What is 'founder-market fit' in one line?
lessons.a: The founders have unusual experience or insight that makes them especially likely to win in this particular market.

lessons.title: Market size: TAM, SAM, SOM
lessons.idea: VCs need the market to be big enough that a winner can be huge.
explain: TAM (total addressable market): all the money spent on this problem everywhere you could ever sell.
SAM (serviceable available market): the part you can actually reach with your product and model.
SOM (serviceable obtainable market): the part you can realistically win in the next few years.
Investors distrust 'TAM is $100 billion' slides. They prefer a bottom-up count: number of customers × what each would pay.
ex: SAM: about 60,000 mid and large offices in India's 8 biggest cities.
Each spends about ₹1.8 lakh a year on tea and snacks.
SAM = 60,000 × ₹1.8 lakh = ₹1,080 crore a year.
SOM: winning 5% in 5 years = 3,000 offices = about ₹54 crore of revenue a year.
A VC would ask: can ChaiCart grow beyond office chai (into office lunches or vending) to make the TAM much bigger?
lessons.investors: Investors want a path to at least a few thousand crore in company value. If the market caps the company at ₹100 crore, it doesn't fit a VC fund's power-law maths.
lessons.q: Why do VCs prefer bottom-up market sizing?
lessons.a: Because it's built from real numbers (customers × price) you can check, instead of a big top-down figure that sounds impressive but proves nothing.

lessons.title: Traction: growth and retention
lessons.idea: Growth shows people want it now. Retention shows they keep wanting it.
explain: Traction means proof that customers want the product: users, orders, revenue.
Growth rate matters more than size early on. 15% growth a month compounds to about 5x in a year.
Retention is the share of customers who keep using you over time. High growth with poor retention is a leaky bucket: you keep pouring in customers who leave.
Investors look at cohorts: group customers by the month they joined and track what share are still active 1, 3 and 6 months later. A good curve flattens out instead of falling to zero.
ex: 100 offices joined in January.
Still ordering after 1 month: 90. After 3 months: 82. After 6 months: 78.
The curve flattens at about 78%. Once an office settles in, it stays. That's a strong sign of product-market fit.
Monthly revenue growth over the last 6 months averaged 15%.
lessons.investors: Investors often care more about retention than growth, because good retention makes all future growth worth more.
lessons.q: Two startups both grow 20% a month. One keeps 80% of customers after 6 months, the other 20%. Which do you fund?
lessons.a: The one with 80% retention. The other is buying growth that leaks away.

lessons.title: Unit economics, burn and runway
lessons.idea: Does each customer make money over time, and how long until the cash runs out?
explain: CAC (customer acquisition cost): what you spend in sales and marketing to win one customer.
LTV (lifetime value): the gross profit a customer brings over their whole time with you.
A common rule of thumb: LTV should be at least 3x CAC, and you should earn back the CAC within about 12 months (the payback period).
Burn rate: how much cash the company loses each month. Runway: how many months until the bank balance hits zero (cash ÷ monthly burn).
ex: Each office orders ₹3,000 a month. After ingredients and delivery, ChaiCart keeps 30%: ₹900 a month of gross profit.
Offices stay about 18 months on average. LTV = ₹900 × 18 = ₹16,200.
Winning an office costs ₹5,400 in sales effort and free trial days. CAC = ₹5,400.
LTV ÷ CAC = 3x. Payback = ₹5,400 ÷ ₹900 = 6 months. Healthy.
Burn: spends ₹60 lakh a month and earns ₹20 lakh of gross profit, so net burn is ₹40 lakh. With ₹4 crore in the bank, runway = 10 months.
lessons.investors: Investors want 18–24 months of runway after a round, because raising the next round takes 6 months and can go wrong. With 10 months left, ChaiCart should start fundraising now.
lessons.q: If ChaiCart's CAC doubled to ₹10,800, what happens to LTV ÷ CAC and payback?
lessons.a: LTV ÷ CAC drops to 1.5x and payback stretches to 12 months. Growth would now cost much more, and investors would worry.

lessons.title: The pitch and due diligence
lessons.idea: The pitch gets a meeting; due diligence decides the deal.
explain: A pitch deck tells a simple story in about 10–15 slides: the problem, the solution, why now, the market, traction, the business model, the competition, the team, and how much money you want and what for.
If the VC is interested, partners meet the founders, then the firm's partners decide together in a partner meeting.
Due diligence is the checking phase: customer calls, financial checks, legal checks (who owns the code and the brand), and background checks on founders.
The process from first meeting to money in the bank often takes 1–3 months. It's slower when the market is cautious.
ex: Week 1: Arjun pitched 12 VC firms; 5 asked for second meetings.
Week 3: Growth Capital's partner spent a day riding with delivery staff and calling 15 office managers.
Week 5: partner meeting said yes, and Growth Capital sent a term sheet (next week's topic).
Weeks 6–10: legal and financial checks, then the money arrived.
lessons.investors: VCs look for consistency: do the deck, the numbers in the books and what customers say all match? One mismatch can kill trust.
lessons.q: What's the difference between a pitch and due diligence?
lessons.a: The pitch is the founders' story to win interest. Due diligence is the investor checking that the story is true.

lessons.title: The cap table: the company's ownership register
lessons.idea: A cap table lists every owner, how many shares they hold and their percentage, round by round.
explain: Cap table is short for capitalisation table. It's a spreadsheet of who owns what.
It includes founders, investors, and the employee stock option pool (shares set aside for employees, next lesson).
'Fully diluted' means counting everything that could become a share, such as options and convertible notes, not just shares already issued. Investors always use fully diluted numbers.
A messy cap table, with too many tiny investors, unclear promises or a founder who left holding a big stake, can scare off future investors.
ex: Each round, new shares are created, and everyone before is diluted by the new investor's percentage.
Total money raised: ₹50 lakh + ₹3 crore + ₹20 crore = ₹23.5 crore.
The founders still own 57.6% together of a company valued at ₹100 crore.
lessons.investors: Before investing, VCs check the cap table to see whether founders still own enough to stay motivated and whether there's any surprise owner or promise.
lessons.q: Why do investors care about 'fully diluted' ownership?
lessons.a: Because options and convertible notes will become shares later and dilute everyone. Ignoring them overstates what each person really owns.

lessons.title: ESOPs and the option pool trick
lessons.idea: Startups reserve shares for employees, and who pays for that reserve matters a lot.
explain: Startups can't pay big salaries, so they offer ESOPs (employee stock options): the right to buy shares later at a fixed low price.
Options usually vest over 4 years with a 1-year cliff: leave before 1 year and you get nothing; after that you earn your options gradually.
Investors usually ask the company to create or top up an option pool (often 10–15%) as part of a funding round.

The trick: if the pool is counted inside the pre-money, existing owners (mainly founders) absorb all its dilution, and the new investor isn't diluted by it at all. It quietly lowers the real price the investor pays.
lessons.ex_title: What if Growth Capital had demanded a 10% pool?
ex: Headline terms unchanged: ₹20 crore at ₹80 crore pre-money, ₹100 crore post-money.
But a new 10% pool must exist after the round, created before the money comes in.
Post-round: Growth Capital 20%, pool 10%, existing owners only 70% instead of 80%.
Each founder ends with 36% × 70% = 25.2% instead of 28.8%.
The existing owners' shares are effectively valued at ₹70 crore, not ₹80 crore. The 'effective pre-money' is lower than the headline.
lessons.investors: Founders should negotiate the pool size using a real hiring plan ('we need ₹X of options for these 12 hires'), not accept a large default.
lessons.q: Why does the option pool's placement (pre- vs post-money) matter to founders?
lessons.a: If it's in the pre-money, founders alone pay for the employees' slice, which lowers the real value of their shares.

lessons.title: SAFEs and convertible notes: investing without setting a price
lessons.idea: Early investors can put in money now and decide the share price later, at the next priced round.
explain: Agreeing a valuation for a tiny startup is hard and legally expensive. So early money often comes in as a promise to convert into shares later.

A convertible note is technically a loan that converts into shares at the next priced round. A SAFE (simple agreement for future equity, created by Y Combinator) is similar but isn't a loan: no interest, no repayment date.

To reward the early risk, these usually have a valuation cap (the maximum valuation at which the money converts) and/or a discount (for example, 20% off the next round's price). The investor gets whichever is better for them.

In India, the US-style SAFE doesn't fit local rules well, so Indian startups usually use instruments like CCPS (compulsorily convertible preference shares) or CCDs (compulsorily convertible debentures). Some platforms offer India-specific 'iSAFE' notes built on these.
lessons.ex_title: If Mehta had used a SAFE instead
ex: Mehta puts in ₹50 lakh on a SAFE with a ₹4 crore cap and a 20% discount.
Later, Seedling prices the seed round at ₹12 crore pre-money.
Discount option: Mehta pays 80% of Seedling's price, as if the company were worth ₹9.6 crore.
Cap option: he converts as if the company were worth only ₹4 crore. Much better, so the cap applies.
He gets roughly 3 times as many shares per rupee as Seedling: about 12.5% before the seed dilution (₹50 lakh ÷ ₹4 crore), instead of the 10% he got in the priced angel round.
lessons.investors: Founders should add up all their SAFEs and notes before the next round. Many small caps add up to a surprise amount of dilution on conversion day.
lessons.q: A SAFE has a ₹10 crore cap and a 20% discount. The next round is priced at ₹8 crore. Which applies?
lessons.a: The discount: 80% of ₹8 crore = ₹6.4 crore, which is lower (better for the investor) than the ₹10 crore cap.

lessons.title: Liquidation preference: who gets paid first
lessons.idea: If the company is sold, investors with a preference get their money back before founders get anything.
explain: Investors usually buy 'preference shares', not ordinary shares. One key right is the liquidation preference: in a sale (or shutdown), they get paid first.
The standard is '1x non-participating': the investor chooses either to get its money back (1x) OR to convert to ordinary shares and take its percentage of the sale. Whichever is more.
'Participating' preferences are much tougher: the investor takes its money back AND its percentage of what's left. Founders should push back on these.
Preferences matter most in modest exits. In a huge exit, everyone converts to ordinary shares and the preference doesn't matter.
lessons.ex_title: ChaiCart is sold for only ₹60 crore after the Series A
ex: Growth Capital (₹20 crore invested, 20% stake, 1x non-participating) chooses the better of ₹20 crore back or 20% × ₹60 crore = ₹12 crore. It takes ₹20 crore.
₹40 crore is left for the other 80% of owners.
Each founder (28.8% of the company) gets 28.8 ÷ 80 × ₹40 crore = ₹14.4 crore.
Without any preference, each founder would have got 28.8% × ₹60 crore = ₹17.28 crore.
lessons.investors: Investors use preferences to protect against overpaying. Founders should watch the multiple (1x vs 2x) and whether it's participating; those two details change the outcome most.
lessons.q: If ChaiCart sold for ₹500 crore, would Growth Capital use its preference?
lessons.a: No. 20% of ₹500 crore is ₹100 crore, far more than its ₹20 crore back, so it converts and shares like everyone else.

lessons.title: Control terms: board seats, vesting and anti-dilution
lessons.idea: Beyond price, a term sheet decides who controls the company and what happens when things go wrong.
explain: Board seats: the board makes the biggest decisions, like hiring or firing the CEO and approving fundraising. A Series A lead usually takes one seat; founders try to keep a majority early on.
Protective provisions (veto rights): investors can block certain actions, such as selling the company or issuing new shares, without their approval.
Founder vesting: investors may ask founders' own shares to 'vest' over time, so a co-founder who leaves early doesn't walk away with a huge stake.
Anti-dilution: if a future round happens at a lower price, protected investors get extra shares. 'Broad-based weighted average' is the normal, gentler version; 'full ratchet' is harsh and rare.
Pro-rata rights (Week 3) and information rights (regular financial reports) are also standard.
ex: ₹20 crore at ₹80 crore pre-money, 1x non-participating liquidation preference.
Board: 2 founders + 1 Growth Capital partner + 1 independent person both sides agree on.
Veto on selling the company or raising new money below this price.
Founders re-vest 25% of their shares over 2 years.
Broad-based weighted average anti-dilution, plus pro-rata rights.
lessons.investors: Experienced founders often say: 'A fair price with clean terms beats a high price with nasty terms.' Terms decide what you actually take home.
lessons.q: Why might a founder accept a lower valuation to avoid a participating 2x preference?
lessons.a: Because harsh preference terms can take far more money in a modest exit than a few crore of valuation difference ever gives back.

lessons.title: Exits: how everyone finally gets paid
lessons.idea: Paper value turns into cash only through an exit: an acquisition, an IPO or a secondary sale.
explain: Acquisition: a bigger company buys the startup. It's the most common exit.
IPO (initial public offering): the company lists on a stock exchange like NSE or BSE, and investors can sell shares in the market, usually after a lock-in period.
Secondary sale: an existing investor or founder sells shares to a new investor before any IPO. It's a way to give early people some cash along the way.
The 'waterfall' is the order in which sale money flows: debts first, then liquidation preferences, then everyone by percentage.
lessons.ex_title: ChaiCart is acquired for ₹500 crore (no further rounds, to keep it simple)
ex: At this price every investor converts, so preferences don't matter. Everyone gets their percentage.
Each founder: 28.8% → ₹144 crore. Mehta: 6.4% → ₹32 crore, 64x his ₹50 lakh.
Seedling: 16% → ₹80 crore, about 27x its ₹3 crore. Growth Capital: 20% → ₹100 crore, 5x its ₹20 crore.
Notice: the earliest, riskiest money earned the biggest multiple.
lessons.investors: Investors think about exits from day one: who could buy this company, and could it plausibly list on a stock exchange?
lessons.q: Why did Mehta earn 64x while Growth Capital earned 5x on the same exit?
lessons.a: Mehta invested at a ₹5 crore valuation, Growth Capital at ₹100 crore. Earlier money buys at a much lower price, which is the reward for taking more risk.

lessons.title: Down rounds and when things go wrong
lessons.idea: Not every round goes up. A lower valuation than last time is a down round, and it's painful.
explain: A down round means raising money at a lower price per share than the previous round. It happens when growth disappoints or markets turn cautious, as in 2022–23 when many startups' valuations fell.

It hurts in three ways: heavy dilution, anti-dilution clauses giving earlier investors extra shares (diluting founders and employees more), and low morale because employees' options may now be worth little.
Alternatives: cut costs to stretch runway, raise a smaller 'bridge' round from existing investors, sell the company, or in the worst case shut down.
Many great companies went through a down round and recovered. It's a setback, not automatically the end.
ex: A big food company launches free office chai and ChaiCart's growth stalls.
ChaiCart needs ₹15 crore. The best offer is at a ₹60 crore pre-money, below the ₹100 crore post-money of the Series A.
Growth Capital's anti-dilution clause gives it extra shares to make up part of the price drop, so the founders are diluted extra.
The founders cut costs, refocus on their most loyal 400 offices, and accept the round to survive.
lessons.investors: Investors judge founders by how they handle bad news: early, honest updates with a plan earn trust for the next round.
lessons.q: Why does a down round hurt employees, not just founders?
lessons.a: Their stock options were priced at the old, higher value, so they may now be worth little or nothing, which can push good people to leave.

lessons.title: Venture capital in India
lessons.idea: The same ideas apply in India, with some local rules and quirks.
explain: Most Indian VC funds are registered with SEBI as Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs). Venture capital and angel funds fall under Category I.
Many big funds investing in India are set up abroad and invest through foreign investment routes, so they follow RBI's foreign exchange rules on pricing and instruments.
Instruments: Indian startups usually issue CCPS (preference shares that must convert to ordinary shares) to investors, rather than US-style preferred stock or SAFEs.
Angel tax: India used to tax startups when they raised money above a 'fair value'. It was a big pain for founders, and it was scrapped in the July 2024 Budget.
Exits: India's IPO market has become a real exit route for startups in recent years, alongside acquisitions.
ex: A US-based fund investing in ChaiCart would invest via the foreign direct investment route, with the price backed by a valuation report as Indian rules require.
It would receive CCPS that convert to ordinary shares later, carrying the preference rights you learned about.
Many Indian startups also 'flip' (move their parent company abroad) or 'reverse flip' (move back to India before an IPO). Several big names have moved back to list in India.
lessons.investors: Global investors look at India for its huge digital public infrastructure (UPI, Aadhaar, Account Aggregator) and young consumers, but they watch exit routes and regulation closely.
lessons.q: Why do Indian startups usually issue CCPS instead of SAFEs?
lessons.a: Because Indian rules, especially for foreign investment, recognise convertible instruments like CCPS and CCDs, while the US-style SAFE doesn't fit those rules well.

lessons.title: Think like a VC: evaluate a deal end to end
lessons.idea: Put it all together: team, market, traction, economics, price and terms.
explain: Step 1: Could this return the fund? Estimate the best-case company value and what your stake would be worth.
Step 2: Why this team, why now?
Step 3: Evidence: growth, retention cohorts, unit economics.
Step 4: Price and terms: what you pay, what you own after future dilution, and your downside protection.
Step 5: The biggest risk, and what would have to be true for it to work.
lessons.ex_title: Monsoon's Series B memo on ChaiCart (illustrative)
ex: Ask: ₹60 crore at a ₹340 crore pre-money (₹400 crore post), so Monsoon would own 15%.
Best case: ChaiCart becomes the default office food platform, worth ₹5,000 crore in 7 years.
After about 30% more dilution in future rounds, 15% becomes about 10.5%, worth ₹525 crore: about 8.75x on ₹60 crore.
Monsoon's fund is ₹400 crore. A ₹525 crore outcome would return more than the whole fund, which passes the test.
Biggest risk: large food delivery apps launching the same service. What must be true: office contracts and 10-minute logistics are hard to copy.
lessons.investors: Every VC memo answers: how big can it get, why will this team win, what's the evidence, what's the price, and what could kill it.
lessons.q: Why does the memo reduce 15% to 10.5% before valuing the outcome?
lessons.a: Because future rounds will dilute Monsoon too. VCs always estimate their ownership at exit, not just at entry.

lessons.title: Capstone: using VC thinking as a PM, and in interviews
lessons.idea: VC thinking is a sharp lens for product strategy, fintech and AI-lab interviews.
explain: As a PM, you can use the VC lens on any feature or product bet: how big could it get, what's the evidence, what does it cost to win each user (CAC), and what's each user worth over time (LTV)?
In fintech, you've seen these instruments up close: lending is debt, while startups raise equity. Knowing both helps you understand why a startup partner behaves the way it does.
AI labs and big tech raise and deploy enormous capital. Knowing how valuations, dilution and investor returns work helps you discuss strategy credibly.
Interview tip: when asked 'Should company X launch Y?', frame it like a VC memo: the size of the prize, why us, the evidence, the costs, the risks, and what would have to be true.
ex: Raised ₹23.5 crore over 3 rounds: angel at ₹5 crore post, seed at ₹15 crore, Series A at ₹100 crore.
Founders went from 100% to 57.6% together, while their stake's value went from nothing to ₹57.6 crore on paper.
Funds win through the power law. Preferences and terms decide modest exits; percentages decide big ones.
Next step: take any startup in the news and ask: what round is this, what's the pre- and post-money, who's diluted, and what must be true for the investors to win?
lessons.investors: You now think like an investor: return the fund, back the team, trust retention, check the unit economics, read the terms, and plan for the exit.
lessons.q: A news story says 'Startup Z raises ₹100 crore at a ₹900 crore valuation'. What two questions do you ask first?
lessons.a: Is ₹900 crore pre- or post-money (so did the investors get 10% or about 11.1%)? And what terms came with it, especially liquidation preferences, since terms matter as much as price.
